summary: Defines protocol extensions and procedures for using internal BGP between provider edge and customer edge routers in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs. The goal is to make the VPN transparent to the customer network as far as routing information goes.

plainLanguage.summary: A company can rent a private network from a provider and want it to behave as if it were one big office. This lets the customer's routers and the provider's exchange routes in a way that hides the provider's network.

subtitle: Letting customer routers and provider edge routers swap BGP routes over iBGP, so a BGP/MPLS VPN looks invisible to the customer.

tldr.problem: When external BGP runs between a VPN provider and a customer, AS_PATH gets modified at the boundary and often the customer's AS number is remapped, which causes drawbacks for customer networks that use BGP internally.
tldr.mechanism: PE and CE routers peer over internal BGP, treating the VPN as a route server. A new optional transitive attribute, ATTR_SET (type code 128), stores the customer's original BGP attributes while the route crosses the VPN, and restores them at the far side.
tldr.outcome: The VPN becomes transparent to the customer as far as routing information is concerned. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 7606 and RFC 9494.

today: RFC 6368 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7606 and RFC 9494, so read those alongside it. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Today, BGP between a provider edge (PE) router and a customer edge (CE) router is typically configured as an external peering between the VPN provider's autonomous system (AS) and the customer's AS. At each boundary the BGP path attributes of RFC 4271 are modified under the standard rules, including prepending the AS numbers of the originating CE and the PE routers to AS_PATH.

To keep AS_PATH loop detection from rejecting such routes, a PE often remaps the customer AS number to its own. Otherwise the customer must use different AS numbers at different sites or accept routes that contain its own AS number. This works when there are no BGP exchanges between the customer and other networks, but has drawbacks for customers that use BGP internally for other purposes.

The RFC therefore defines a way for PE and CE routers to exchange BGP routes by means other than External BGP. It treats the VPN as a provider-managed backbone interconnecting customer-managed sites, similar to hierarchies built with route reflection (RFC 4456) or confederations (RFC 5065).
sections.plainLanguage: Today the delivery company changes the labels on every note it carries. That confuses offices that use those labels for their own business, so this RFC finds a way to deliver notes untouched.

sections.title: The VPN as a Route Server
sections.content:
In a normal backbone and area design, routers that attach an area to the core use route reflection or confederations to pass routes between the core iBGP mesh and the local area. The RFC proposes viewing the VPN as the equivalent of an Internal BGP Route Server that multiplexes information from N VPN attachment points.

A route learned by any PE is available to all other PEs that import the Route Target identifying the customer network. A PE does not advertise PE-received routes back to other PEs. This split-horizon technique prevents routing loops, and matches the behavior of a top-level mesh of route reflectors.

On a PE, a CE-received route MUST be advertised to other VPN PEs that import the associated Route Targets, whether the CE route was received as internal or external. It is not re-advertised to other CEs unless route reflection is explicitly configured, which is the equivalent of disabling client-to-client reflection. When the PE reflects with local CEs as clients, those CEs do not need to be meshed. The RFC chooses not to describe a confederation-style variant in detail.
sections.plainLanguage: The delivery company acts like one big bulletin board. Every office posts its news, every other office can read it, and nobody gets their own news handed back.

sections.title: Pushing and Popping Path Attributes
sections.content:
Attributes behave like a stack. When a route enters the VPN, the PE pushes the attributes received from the customer network onto the stack before adding the Export Route Targets, as part of the RFC 4364 route processing. At the other end, the stack is popped after the Import Target processing step that picks the VRF accepting the route.

At the vrf-export stage the advertising PE SHOULD initialize the attributes of the VPN route as it would for a locally originated route in that VRF. When a PE-received route is imported, its IGP metric for path selection SHOULD be the metric to the remote PE address, in the provider's metric domain. Customer IGP metrics SHOULD always be considered higher, and thus less preferred, than local site metrics.

When a CE reflects a PE-received route to another PE, the preserved original attributes prevent loops caused by mutual redistribution between the two networks. With backdoor links, traffic tends to use the backdoor for routes originated by a remote site, but BGP policy such as LOCAL_PREF can address that.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a stack of plates. The first office puts its labels on the stack, the delivery company carries the stack, and the second office takes the labels off the top again.

sections.title: The ATTR_SET Attribute
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new BGP path attribute, ATTR_SET, type code 128. It is an optional transitive attribute that carries a set of BGP attributes. It can include any attribute that can occur in an UPDATE message except MP_REACH and MP_UNREACH.

The value is a 4-octet Origin AS followed by the encoded path attributes, so its length is 4 plus the length of the encoded attributes. Flags follow RFC 4271, and the Extended Length bit decides whether the length field is one or two octets. Origin AS SHOULD hold the AS number of the customer network that originated the attributes, as a 32-bit unsigned integer in network byte order, whether or not the PE supports 4-octet AS numbers. AS_PATH and AGGREGATOR inside an ATTR_SET MUST use 4-octet AS numbers (RFC 4893), and speakers supporting this RFC MUST support RFC 4893.

The PE stores the attributes received from a CE in ATTR_SET, and uses them when it advertises a PE-received route to a CE. This isolates the customer's attributes from the provider's. For instance, route reflection cluster lists are kept apart, so customer cluster identifiers are not seen by provider route reflectors and the reverse. NEXT_HOP SHOULD NOT be included, and if present SHOULD be ignored by the receiving PE.

An ATTR_SET is malformed if it is shorter than 4 octets, includes MP_REACH or MP_UNREACH, or contains malformed attributes. If the Partial flag is set and the Neighbor-Complete flag is clear, the UPDATE is treated as a withdraw. Otherwise the Optional Attribute Error procedures of RFC 4271 MUST be followed.
sections.plainLanguage: ATTR_SET is the sealed envelope. Inside it are the customer's original labels plus a note saying which office wrote them.

sections.title: Next-Hop Handling
sections.content:
Without VPNs, the NEXT_HOP of an iBGP route is the border router that advertised it into the domain, and IGP distance to it matters for selection. With a VPN, customer sites run different IGP domains, so provider and customer metrics are not comparable.

The RFC says the most important metric component is the inter-area metric, which the customer network knows, while the intra-area metric is typically negligible. It rewrites NEXT_HOP at the VRF import and export boundary. PEs take into account the PE-to-PE IGP distance calculated by the customer network IGP when choosing between routes from different PEs. A benefit is that the customer can run independent IGPs at each site.
sections.plainLanguage: Each office measures distances its own way, so the two measurements cannot be added up directly. The RFC says to rewrite the 'next stop' on the way in and out and rely on the customer's own sense of which route is far.

sections.title: Routes Between Different Customer ASes
sections.content:
With iBGP PE-CE sessions, the VRF that connects to a customer site is assigned to the customer AS rather than the provider AS. The Origin AS in ATTR_SET tells the receiving PE which AS the route came from, so it can spot exchanges between VRFs in different ASes, as in an extranet VPN.

On import into a VRF, a PE MUST compare the Origin AS with the VRF's AS. If they match, the route is imported with the attributes from ATTR_SET. If they differ, the PE builds the attributes as if the two ASes had an External BGP session: take the attributes from ATTR_SET, discard iBGP-specific ones such as LOCAL_PREF, ORIGINATOR and CLUSTER_LIST, prepend the Origin AS to AS_PATH, and if the VRF's AS is the provider AS and the VPN route's AS_PATH is not empty, prepend that AS_PATH too.

When advertising a VRF route to an External BGP peer, the PE applies the same four steps and then prepends its own AS. Importing a route without ATTR_SET into a VRF in a different AS MUST prepend the provider AS number. Whenever ATTR_SET is present, all other attributes on the VPN route except NEXT_HOP are ignored, so ATTR_SET overrides them on vrf-import.
sections.plainLanguage: If the envelope goes to an office of the same company, it is opened as it was written. If it goes to a different company, the delivery company adds a note saying who wrote it first.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
It is RECOMMENDED that different VRFs of the same VPN, on different PEs, that use iBGP PE-CE sessions have different Route Distinguisher values. With the same RD, the VPN infrastructure may select a single customer path for a prefix without seeing the details in ATTR_SET. In the route server model this implies unique RDs per VRF.

The extension isolates the customer from the provider's attribute operations and the provider from attributes injected by the customer. For example, BGP communities that influence the VPN infrastructure can be carried transparently. It also helps when the same provider AS number is used for Internet service and the IP VPN, where a customer route may contain the provider's AS number.

For VPN backbones that span several ASes, options b) and c) of Section 10 of RFC 4364 can provide a transparent service. With option a), there is no way to provide full transparency to the customer AS.
sections.plainLanguage: Give every office its own return address, so the bulletin board can tell their notes apart.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
For the provider, the mechanism separates the BGP attributes advertised by a CE from those used inside the provider network, which can improve security. Without it, a CE may be able to inject attributes such as extended communities that have meaning in the provider network, unless the PE configuration prevents it. With ATTR_SET, every attribute received from a CE is pushed onto the stack. Implementations must still consider input validation and resource management.

For the customer, the authors say they believe the security profile of PE-CE interaction does not change. An iBGP session lets the PE set attributes such as LOCAL_PREF that External BGP does not allow, but the customer already has to trust the provider to give it correct routing information.
sections.plainLanguage: Sealing notes in envelopes stops a sender from slipping in secret instructions for the delivery company. The customer still has to trust the delivery company to hand over the right notes.
